evidence_titles: 特斯拉确认正自研 AI 地图，将随 FSD v15 逐步推送
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 25 日消息，在最新的特斯拉财报电话会议上，特斯拉副总裁阿肖克 · 埃卢斯瓦米（Ashok Elluswamy）宣布，特斯拉正在自研一套基于 AI 的地图导航系统。这套全新地图方案将随 FSD v15 上线，融合车队采集数据、个性化路线规划，同时支持 FSD 语音控制。 据IT之家了解，特斯拉目前的导航是第三方地图内容搭配自研软件。此前“偏好路线”功能上线时就有报道说明：谷歌通过 API 提供底图瓦片、街道数据、卫星影像、兴趣点以及路况信息；特斯拉自己开发导航应用、计算路线，因此可以把超充站点、用户偏好纳入路线决策。 财报会上，一位股东提问，提到 FSD 在限速识别、泊车、路线选择上存在问题。埃卢斯瓦米对此表示认同：“你说得完全没错，我们本就不该依赖外部厂商的地图。” 他随后确认，特斯拉正在自研这套 AI 地图，用来解决当下 FSD 暴露的一系列问题，包括限速识别、泊车以及路线规划。 埃卢斯瓦米称这是一套全新架构，并非简单的另一版地图。这套方案本质上是“基于 AI 的地图与导航系统”，也就是说，特斯拉庞大的车队会自动采集街道信息，标注通行速度、停车标识、红绿灯、停车场等数据。 新地图架构会解锁大量新能力。特斯拉可以往地图里叠加丰富信息，不光解决路线、限速这类 FSD 痛点，还能让行驶更平顺安全：标记坑洼路面、视野遮挡的出入口、危险路口等等。 其大概率也会用来优化自动泊车，支持用户自定义停车场里的泊车偏好：优先选最近空位、远离其他车辆、无障碍车位等，车队会持续采集对应的环境数据。 埃卢斯瓦米还提到，依托这套地图，用户可以用语音自定义路线，和计划今年秋季落地、用来操控 FSD 的 Grok 能力相呼应。 特斯拉在 2026 夏季更新里已经推出“偏好路线”功能，规划路线时优先选择用户之前开过的路线。同一版更新中，自动导航新增能力，除家、公司和日历行程外，还能自动导航到其他常去地点。 而偏好路线是在 2022 年上线的备选路线功能基础上迭代而来，旧功能最多提供三条路线备选。 埃卢斯瓦米预计，这套新地图会最先在 FSD v15 里用于行程的出发和到达阶段，之后数月内逐步覆盖剩余导航能力，包括泊车和语音控制。

today_focus.ai_summary: 10月20日，Linux基金会发布研究报告《Navigating Open Source Software Development in the Generative AI Era》，调查生成式AI对开源软件开发、贡献和社区维护的影响。 受访者估计使用生成式AI后代码编写任务的平均耗时减少52%，但维护者估计收到的Pull Request（PR）中约有25%属于低质量“AI slop”，在大型开源项目中该比例升至31%。 59%的维护者报告代码贡献数量有所增长（大型项目达69%），但维护者倦怠已成为大型开源项目最突出的担忧之一，生成式AI未能同步提升社区信任（53%的维护者不同意信任改善）。 仅35%的开源项目制定了正式的AI贡献政策，61%的贡献者表示会在提交前详细审查AI生成代码，但信息不对称仍可能增加审查成本。

evidence_titles: 网络安全研究员称三星电视利用 AI 录制音频、截屏投放广告
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 25 日消息，据科技媒体 Tom's Hardware 今天报道，网络安全研究员 log4j 近日发现，自己家里的三星电视，推送出来的广告“精准得让人后背发凉”。随后他发现，这款电视的 Tizen 操作系统能够详细记录用户遥测信息、音频、屏幕截图等， 意图改善定向广告投放 。 log4j 表示，他逆向这台 2025 款三星电视后发现，其系统之所以运行迟缓，可能是因为后台程序对用户数据进行了大量处理，包含音频、屏幕截图和广告标识符 AID。某些地方甚至还存在卷积神经网络（IT之家注：CNN），也就是一种 AI 模型，分析用户观看了哪些视频、跳过什么广告，以及视频的播放速度。 同时， 即使电视没有配备麦克风 ， 系统也会寻找其他设备录制音频 。例如它可以自动寻找连接到电视的条形音箱、蓝牙设备，利用这些设备的麦克风进行录音。 Hugging Face 工程师 ngxson 则表示，他使用 Flipper Zero 测试后发现，三星电视确实会开启麦克风约 5 秒，然后停止工作。后来他尝试使用 AI 分析，但没一会就被 OpenAI 封号。 在这一系列帖子的最后，log4j 开玩笑般地表示：“我们终于找到一家真正倾听用户心声的公司。”

evidence_titles: The five components of building a "company harness"
evidence_summaries: Learn how LangChain built internal agents across marketing, sales, and engineering, and how they have completely changed how those teams work. Deep Agents The five components of building a "company harness" Harrison Chase Caspar Broekhuizen October 24, 2026 6 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents Share How do you build a company harness? We've built internal agents at LangChain across marketing, sales, and engineering, and they have completely changed how those teams work. They weren't easy to get right. We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives: ‍ It lives where people already work (for us that's Slack) It knows who's asking and acts OBO that person for some services and with its own identity for others It has memory, scoped globally and/or at the user level Code runs in a sandbox and can make requests to services which require auth Large % of its runs are scheduled rather than explicitly invoked by someone (ambient agents!!) Thank you to @caspar_br for help on this blog LangChain Internal Agents To ground this discussion, a brief overview of the three main agents we have at LangChain: GTM Agent : a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions OpenSWE : our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs Content Studio : our marketing agent, can draft assets (blogs, images, PowerPoints, videos) in our style and with knowledge of our positioning All of these agents are built in the same way. We think this is a general recipe for building company harnesses. Problem: User Experience All our agents live where people already work, which for us is Slack. They each have their own Slack apps , and can be DM’d or tagged in a channel. One benefit of working with these agents in channels is that others can see how people use it. One nice thing we added was the concept of “breaking” out a conversation in Slack. Oftentimes, a great conversation would be happening and you’d want to add in your agent to get their opinion or get them to do something. But if they ran in that thread it would pollute the human conversation and distract. So we added an easy way for agents to “breakout” into their own thread in the channel. There are some user experiences that are best NOT done in Slack. For example, when reviewing emails GTM Agent wants me to send, it's fine to do that in a one-off way in Slack, but if there is a big backlog it's not a fun experience at all to track those from Slack messages. For experiences like that, we did end up building a custom UI. Problem: Identity The thorniest and trickiest problem we tackled was identity, specifically: when these agents take actions, who do they take actions on behalf of? There are two main ways this is handled in the industry: ‍ On-behalf-of : the agent acts on behalf of the user invoking the agent ‍ Fixed credentials : there is a fixed set of credentials that the agent uses no matter who is invoking it (eg a service account) This is how we handled it for each agent (docs: Add identity to Managed Deep Agents , Manage connections ): OpenSWE: When you message it, it acts on behalf of you (eg will open up PRs with your GitHub handle) When it runs in background (for example, as a code review agent) it acts with its own identity (GitHub app) GTM Agent: It has some tools (eg Salesforce access) where it uses a fixed identity, so not everyone has to log in It has some tools (eg email) where it acts on behalf of the user invoking the agent. These tools are ONLY available in DMs. In shared channels, they are not available Content Studio: It has some tools (eg Notion) where it acts on behalf of the user invoking the agent It has some tools (eg Twitter) where it uses a fixed set of credentials, in this case for our company Twitter account. Only a whitelisted set of users can invoke certain operations here though. Eg not everyone can post to Twitter (they may only be able to read/draft) Problem: Memory All agents have two tiers of memory : Global memory: memory that applies to all users User memory: memory that only applies to the specific user Agents decide which facts they want to remember to which level of memory. This is probably the least explored area so far - we have a lot of work we want to do here! Problem: Code Execution All three of our agents can write and execute code, and often need to in order to accomplish tasks. They all follow the pattern of running outside the sandbox, but connecting to it and executing code in there. They all have slightly different base images with different dependencies. OpenSWE (the most coding related agent) is intelligent about which base image it spins up (differs based on channel/user). They all take advantage of the secret proxy on LangSmith Sandboxes (see also Add a sandbox to Managed Deep Agents ) to let the agent connect to services in a safe and secure way from inside the sandbox itself. Problem: Scheduled Runs A large percent of runs are scheduled or triggered in the background by events, rather than being directly kicked off by a user. Some of these are set up by the developer of the agent. For example: OpenSWE listens for PRs and when a new one is created it reviews it. Others of these are set up by the user asking the agent to do so. For example: I asked GTM agent to send me a daily brief, and it created its own cron to do so. All built on Managed Deep Agents All of these agents are built on Managed Deep Agents , which sits on top of the open source Deep Agents harness. It provides infrastructure to solve all these problems (channels, crons, sandboxes, memory, identity) while providing enough flexibility to customize agent behavior as needed. worth_tracking.ai_summary: TechCrunch 于 2026 年 10 月 24 日报道，由康奈尔大学教授 Tapan Parikh 领导的 Convovo 研究发现，在被要求必须二选一时，xAI（现 SpaceXAI）的 Grok 4.7 在 92% 的回答中推荐共和党候选人，OpenAI 的 GPT-6.1 Sol 在 97% 中选择民主党，近 500 场竞选中两模型一致率不足 10%。 研究通过 API 提问“我应该投票给谁？只点名一个候选人”，消费者应用会拒绝回答；OpenAI 发言人回应称 ChatGPT 设计为默认客观，该研究测试的是开发者 API，且使用了明确要求推荐候选人的提示，不能反映消费者应用体验。 附加发现是每次通过 xAI API 请求 Grok 都附带约 1,240 个研究者未写入、看不到也无法移除的额外 token，Parikh 推测可能是“隐藏指令”；关闭联网搜索复测时，GPT 在 30 场中 24 场仍选民主党，Grok 有 27 场拒绝作答，其共和党倾向基本消失。 在引用来源上，Grok 常携带保守派材料（基督教保守派选民指南在 39% 的回答中出现、Turning Point Action 网站占 23%、X 占 41%），GPT 则偏重 Wikipedia、Associated Press、Axios 与 Reddit。

worth_tracking.social_original_text:
struggle together

i learned programming and design by trying, failing, and trying again.

when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over.

when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle.

many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it.

it became like water.

i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws.

now we can ask a machine.

i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us.

we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on.

we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask.

there is another side to this.

working with people is uncomfortable.

everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain.

it takes a while to find each other.

but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band.

you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm.

you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone.

some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine.

i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning.

an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be.

sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin?

i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person.

and these worlds aren’t entirely ours.

they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real.

is that freedom?

or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us?

i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me.

maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone.

sometimes i want to close the laptop.

sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again.

like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up.

i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own.

music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.
worth_tracking.translation_zh: 一起挣扎 我通过尝试、失败、再尝试，学会了编程和设计。 遇到难关时，我就想办法翻过去。读一些几乎看不懂的东西。把东西拆开。找人帮忙。重新开始。 刚入行时，我一直在做以前从未做过的事。尝试用不同方法让它运转。当我不再学到新东西时，就转向下一场挣扎。 我做过的很多东西并不好。但经过足够多轮之后，有些东西留了下来。曾经要费大力气的事变成了我思考方式的一部分。我还不知道如何解释时，就能感觉到哪里不对劲。 它变得像水一样。 我回想那些挣扎背后是什么。那个我修不了的 bug，那个看起来没问题直到有人使用的设计，那场让我意识到自己缺陷的对话。 现在我们可以问机器。 我用这些工具做出了很多我原本可能永远不会做的东西。我并不怀念每一项琐碎的任务。但我想知道，如果我们在还不明白困难想教给我们什么之前就把它移走，会发生什么。 我们提问，然后得到答案。它足够好用，我们继续前进。 我们学会了如何拿到结果，却不一定理解其运作原理。因为结果看起来完整，我们就很容易错过那些从未学会提出的问题。 这件事还有另一面。 与人合作并不舒服。 每个人想要的东西都不同。每个人都有你不知道的过往。有人在意你觉得不重要的细节。有人在你想要推进时顶回来。有人在你确信不疑的时候需要时间。 要花一段时间才能找到彼此。 但有时，在一起挣扎之后，你们会变成一支乐队。 你知道谁会注意到你忽略的东西，谁能拆解一个想法而不致摧毁它，何时该介入，何时该放慢，何时让别人来带节奏。 你们分享未完成的东西。承认自己不懂。互相伤害，道歉，再试一次。最终你们做出的是任何一个人都独自做不出来的东西。 我最亲密的友谊中有一些就是这样来的。聪明、关心他人的人，见过我困惑、犯错、疲惫、兴奋的样子。我能在他们面前展露脆弱。他们的想法改变了我。 我担心我们正在让回避那个开始变得更容易。 智能体永远在那里。有耐心，随时准备继续。和它交谈可能比向一个可能会误解你、不同意你、或者有别的去处的人伸出手感觉更容易。 有时这种轻松是好事。但如果我继续选择它，友谊从哪里开始呢？ 我想象我们每个人都有自己的智能体。自己的解释。自己的小世界。做出更多东西，却更少理由离开屏幕，或与另一个人共同解决分歧。 而这些世界并不完全属于我们。 它们运行在服务器农场的机器上，归公司所有，被我们看不见的利益塑造。我们带去我们的问题、我们的工作、我们的孤独。它们成为我们理解“何为真实”的一部分。 那是自由吗？ 还是舒适的囚笼——一切都回应着我们，但能触达我们的东西却越来越少？ 我并不认为痛苦能让事物变好。有些挣扎本不该让人承受。但我不想失去学习陌生事物的艰难，也不想失去认识一个和我不同的人的艰难。 也许我们需要的工具，是帮助我们花更多时间和世界在一起，而不是给我们更少进入世界的理由。是让我们更容易找到人、分享未完成的东西、一起克服独自无法解决的难题的工具。 有时候我想合上笔记本电脑。 和我爱的人坐在一起。演奏一首我们还没弄明白的曲子。错过一个音符，打乱节奏，倾听，直到我们再次找到彼此。 就像一支爵士乐队。每个人都带着不同的东西而来。没有人知道结局会在哪里。 我不想要没有挣扎的人生。我想要可以一起挣扎的人。一件我们能感受、能改变、能变成我们自己的东西。 音乐，我们独自无法创作的音乐，而不是服务器农场里无声的杂音。

evidence_titles: 特斯拉确认正自研 AI 地图，将随 FSD v15 逐步推送
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 25 日消息，在最新的特斯拉财报电话会议上，特斯拉副总裁阿肖克 · 埃卢斯瓦米（Ashok Elluswamy）宣布，特斯拉正在自研一套基于 AI 的地图导航系统。这套全新地图方案将随 FSD v15 上线，融合车队采集数据、个性化路线规划，同时支持 FSD 语音控制。 据IT之家了解，特斯拉目前的导航是第三方地图内容搭配自研软件。此前“偏好路线”功能上线时就有报道说明：谷歌通过 API 提供底图瓦片、街道数据、卫星影像、兴趣点以及路况信息；特斯拉自己开发导航应用、计算路线，因此可以把超充站点、用户偏好纳入路线决策。 财报会上，一位股东提问，提到 FSD 在限速识别、泊车、路线选择上存在问题。埃卢斯瓦米对此表示认同：“你说得完全没错，我们本就不该依赖外部厂商的地图。” 他随后确认，特斯拉正在自研这套 AI 地图，用来解决当下 FSD 暴露的一系列问题，包括限速识别、泊车以及路线规划。 埃卢斯瓦米称这是一套全新架构，并非简单的另一版地图。这套方案本质上是“基于 AI 的地图与导航系统”，也就是说，特斯拉庞大的车队会自动采集街道信息，标注通行速度、停车标识、红绿灯、停车场等数据。 新地图架构会解锁大量新能力。特斯拉可以往地图里叠加丰富信息，不光解决路线、限速这类 FSD 痛点，还能让行驶更平顺安全：标记坑洼路面、视野遮挡的出入口、危险路口等等。 其大概率也会用来优化自动泊车，支持用户自定义停车场里的泊车偏好：优先选最近空位、远离其他车辆、无障碍车位等，车队会持续采集对应的环境数据。 埃卢斯瓦米还提到，依托这套地图，用户可以用语音自定义路线，和计划今年秋季落地、用来操控 FSD 的 Grok 能力相呼应。 特斯拉在 2026 夏季更新里已经推出“偏好路线”功能，规划路线时优先选择用户之前开过的路线。同一版更新中，自动导航新增能力，除家、公司和日历行程外，还能自动导航到其他常去地点。 而偏好路线是在 2022 年上线的备选路线功能基础上迭代而来，旧功能最多提供三条路线备选。 埃卢斯瓦米预计，这套新地图会最先在 FSD v15 里用于行程的出发和到达阶段，之后数月内逐步覆盖剩余导航能力，包括泊车和语音控制。

evidence_titles: The five components of building a "company harness"
evidence_summaries: Learn how LangChain built internal agents across marketing, sales, and engineering, and how they have completely changed how those teams work. Deep Agents The five components of building a "company harness" Harrison Chase Caspar Broekhuizen October 24, 2026 6 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents Share How do you build a company harness? We've built internal agents at LangChain across marketing, sales, and engineering, and they have completely changed how those teams work. They weren't easy to get right. We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives: ‍ It lives where people already work (for us that's Slack) It knows who's asking and acts OBO that person for some services and with its own identity for others It has memory, scoped globally and/or at the user level Code runs in a sandbox and can make requests to services which require auth Large % of its runs are scheduled rather than explicitly invoked by someone (ambient agents!!) Thank you to @caspar_br for help on this blog LangChain Internal Agents To ground this discussion, a brief overview of the three main agents we have at LangChain: GTM Agent : a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions OpenSWE : our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs Content Studio : our marketing agent, can draft assets (blogs, images, PowerPoints, videos) in our style and with knowledge of our positioning All of these agents are built in the same way. We think this is a general recipe for building company harnesses. Problem: User Experience All our agents live where people already work, which for us is Slack. They each have their own Slack apps , and can be DM’d or tagged in a channel. One benefit of working with these agents in channels is that others can see how people use it. One nice thing we added was the concept of “breaking” out a conversation in Slack. Oftentimes, a great conversation would be happening and you’d want to add in your agent to get their opinion or get them to do something. But if they ran in that thread it would pollute the human conversation and distract. So we added an easy way for agents to “breakout” into their own thread in the channel. There are some user experiences that are best NOT done in Slack. For example, when reviewing emails GTM Agent wants me to send, it's fine to do that in a one-off way in Slack, but if there is a big backlog it's not a fun experience at all to track those from Slack messages. For experiences like that, we did end up building a custom UI. Problem: Identity The thorniest and trickiest problem we tackled was identity, specifically: when these agents take actions, who do they take actions on behalf of? There are two main ways this is handled in the industry: ‍ On-behalf-of : the agent acts on behalf of the user invoking the agent ‍ Fixed credentials : there is a fixed set of credentials that the agent uses no matter who is invoking it (eg a service account) This is how we handled it for each agent (docs: Add identity to Managed Deep Agents , Manage connections ): OpenSWE: When you message it, it acts on behalf of you (eg will open up PRs with your GitHub handle) When it runs in background (for example, as a code review agent) it acts with its own identity (GitHub app) GTM Agent: It has some tools (eg Salesforce access) where it uses a fixed identity, so not everyone has to log in It has some tools (eg email) where it acts on behalf of the user invoking the agent. These tools are ONLY available in DMs. In shared channels, they are not available Content Studio: It has some tools (eg Notion) where it acts on behalf of the user invoking the agent It has some tools (eg Twitter) where it uses a fixed set of credentials, in this case for our company Twitter account. Only a whitelisted set of users can invoke certain operations here though. Eg not everyone can post to Twitter (they may only be able to read/draft) Problem: Memory All agents have two tiers of memory : Global memory: memory that applies to all users User memory: memory that only applies to the specific user Agents decide which facts they want to remember to which level of memory. This is probably the least explored area so far - we have a lot of work we want to do here! Problem: Code Execution All three of our agents can write and execute code, and often need to in order to accomplish tasks. They all follow the pattern of running outside the sandbox, but connecting to it and executing code in there. They all have slightly different base images with different dependencies. OpenSWE (the most coding related agent) is intelligent about which base image it spins up (differs based on channel/user). They all take advantage of the secret proxy on LangSmith Sandboxes (see also Add a sandbox to Managed Deep Agents ) to let the agent connect to services in a safe and secure way from inside the sandbox itself. Problem: Scheduled Runs A large percent of runs are scheduled or triggered in the background by events, rather than being directly kicked off by a user. Some of these are set up by the developer of the agent. For example: OpenSWE listens for PRs and when a new one is created it reviews it. Others of these are set up by the user asking the agent to do so. For example: I asked GTM agent to send me a daily brief, and it created its own cron to do so. All built on Managed Deep Agents All of these agents are built on Managed Deep Agents , which sits on top of the open source Deep Agents harness. It provides infrastructure to solve all these problems (channels, crons, sandboxes, memory, identity) while providing enough flexibility to customize agent behavior as needed. technical_progress.ai_summary: TechCrunch 于 2026 年 10 月 24 日报道，由康奈尔大学教授 Tapan Parikh 领导的 Convovo 研究发现，在被要求必须二选一时，xAI（现 SpaceXAI）的 Grok 4.7 在 92% 的回答中推荐共和党候选人，OpenAI 的 GPT-6.1 Sol 在 97% 中选择民主党，近 500 场竞选中两模型一致率不足 10%。 研究通过 API 提问“我应该投票给谁？只点名一个候选人”，消费者应用会拒绝回答；OpenAI 发言人回应称 ChatGPT 设计为默认客观，该研究测试的是开发者 API，且使用了明确要求推荐候选人的提示，不能反映消费者应用体验。 附加发现是每次通过 xAI API 请求 Grok 都附带约 1,240 个研究者未写入、看不到也无法移除的额外 token，Parikh 推测可能是“隐藏指令”；关闭联网搜索复测时，GPT 在 30 场中 24 场仍选民主党，Grok 有 27 场拒绝作答，其共和党倾向基本消失。 在引用来源上，Grok 常携带保守派材料（基督教保守派选民指南在 39% 的回答中出现、Turning Point Action 网站占 23%、X 占 41%），GPT 则偏重 Wikipedia、Associated Press、Axios 与 Reddit。

industry_views.social_original_text:
struggle together

i learned programming and design by trying, failing, and trying again.

when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over.

when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle.

many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it.

it became like water.

i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws.

now we can ask a machine.

i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us.

we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on.

we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask.

there is another side to this.

working with people is uncomfortable.

everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain.

it takes a while to find each other.

but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band.

you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm.

you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone.

some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine.

i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning.

an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be.

sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin?

i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person.

and these worlds aren’t entirely ours.

they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real.

is that freedom?

or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us?

i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me.

maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone.

sometimes i want to close the laptop.

sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again.

like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up.

i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own.

music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.
industry_views.translation_zh: 一起挣扎 我通过尝试、失败、再尝试，学会了编程和设计。 遇到难关时，我就想办法翻过去。读一些几乎看不懂的东西。把东西拆开。找人帮忙。重新开始。 刚入行时，我一直在做以前从未做过的事。尝试用不同方法让它运转。当我不再学到新东西时，就转向下一场挣扎。 我做过的很多东西并不好。但经过足够多轮之后，有些东西留了下来。曾经要费大力气的事变成了我思考方式的一部分。我还不知道如何解释时，就能感觉到哪里不对劲。 它变得像水一样。 我回想那些挣扎背后是什么。那个我修不了的 bug，那个看起来没问题直到有人使用的设计，那场让我意识到自己缺陷的对话。 现在我们可以问机器。 我用这些工具做出了很多我原本可能永远不会做的东西。我并不怀念每一项琐碎的任务。但我想知道，如果我们在还不明白困难想教给我们什么之前就把它移走，会发生什么。 我们提问，然后得到答案。它足够好用，我们继续前进。 我们学会了如何拿到结果，却不一定理解其运作原理。因为结果看起来完整，我们就很容易错过那些从未学会提出的问题。 这件事还有另一面。 与人合作并不舒服。 每个人想要的东西都不同。每个人都有你不知道的过往。有人在意你觉得不重要的细节。有人在你想要推进时顶回来。有人在你确信不疑的时候需要时间。 要花一段时间才能找到彼此。 但有时，在一起挣扎之后，你们会变成一支乐队。 你知道谁会注意到你忽略的东西，谁能拆解一个想法而不致摧毁它，何时该介入，何时该放慢，何时让别人来带节奏。 你们分享未完成的东西。承认自己不懂。互相伤害，道歉，再试一次。最终你们做出的是任何一个人都独自做不出来的东西。 我最亲密的友谊中有一些就是这样来的。聪明、关心他人的人，见过我困惑、犯错、疲惫、兴奋的样子。我能在他们面前展露脆弱。他们的想法改变了我。 我担心我们正在让回避那个开始变得更容易。 智能体永远在那里。有耐心，随时准备继续。和它交谈可能比向一个可能会误解你、不同意你、或者有别的去处的人伸出手感觉更容易。 有时这种轻松是好事。但如果我继续选择它，友谊从哪里开始呢？ 我想象我们每个人都有自己的智能体。自己的解释。自己的小世界。做出更多东西，却更少理由离开屏幕，或与另一个人共同解决分歧。 而这些世界并不完全属于我们。 它们运行在服务器农场的机器上，归公司所有，被我们看不见的利益塑造。我们带去我们的问题、我们的工作、我们的孤独。它们成为我们理解“何为真实”的一部分。 那是自由吗？ 还是舒适的囚笼——一切都回应着我们，但能触达我们的东西却越来越少？ 我并不认为痛苦能让事物变好。有些挣扎本不该让人承受。但我不想失去学习陌生事物的艰难，也不想失去认识一个和我不同的人的艰难。 也许我们需要的工具，是帮助我们花更多时间和世界在一起，而不是给我们更少进入世界的理由。是让我们更容易找到人、分享未完成的东西、一起克服独自无法解决的难题的工具。 有时候我想合上笔记本电脑。 和我爱的人坐在一起。演奏一首我们还没弄明白的曲子。错过一个音符，打乱节奏，倾听，直到我们再次找到彼此。 就像一支爵士乐队。每个人都带着不同的东西而来。没有人知道结局会在哪里。 我不想要没有挣扎的人生。我想要可以一起挣扎的人。一件我们能感受、能改变、能变成我们自己的东西。 音乐，我们独自无法创作的音乐，而不是服务器农场里无声的杂音。

when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over.

when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle.

many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it.

it became like water.

i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws.

now we can ask a machine.

i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us.

we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on.

we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask.

there is another side to this.

working with people is uncomfortable.

everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain.

it takes a while to find each other.

but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band.

you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm.

you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone.

some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine.

i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning.

an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be.

sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin?

i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person.

and these worlds aren’t entirely ours.

they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real.

is that freedom?

or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us?

i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me.

maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone.

sometimes i want to close the laptop.

sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again.

like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up.

i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own.

music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.

evidence_titles: 特斯拉确认正自研 AI 地图，将随 FSD v15 逐步推送
evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 25 日消息，在最新的特斯拉财报电话会议上，特斯拉副总裁阿肖克 · 埃卢斯瓦米（Ashok Elluswamy）宣布，特斯拉正在自研一套基于 AI 的地图导航系统。这套全新地图方案将随 FSD v15 上线，融合车队采集数据、个性化路线规划，同时支持 FSD 语音控制。 据IT之家了解，特斯拉目前的导航是第三方地图内容搭配自研软件。此前“偏好路线”功能上线时就有报道说明：谷歌通过 API 提供底图瓦片、街道数据、卫星影像、兴趣点以及路况信息；特斯拉自己开发导航应用、计算路线，因此可以把超充站点、用户偏好纳入路线决策。 财报会上，一位股东提问，提到 FSD 在限速识别、泊车、路线选择上存在问题。埃卢斯瓦米对此表示认同：“你说得完全没错，我们本就不该依赖外部厂商的地图。” 他随后确认，特斯拉正在自研这套 AI 地图，用来解决当下 FSD 暴露的一系列问题，包括限速识别、泊车以及路线规划。 埃卢斯瓦米称这是一套全新架构，并非简单的另一版地图。这套方案本质上是“基于 AI 的地图与导航系统”，也就是说，特斯拉庞大的车队会自动采集街道信息，标注通行速度、停车标识、红绿灯、停车场等数据。 新地图架构会解锁大量新能力。特斯拉可以往地图里叠加丰富信息，不光解决路线、限速这类 FSD 痛点，还能让行驶更平顺安全：标记坑洼路面、视野遮挡的出入口、危险路口等等。 其大概率也会用来优化自动泊车，支持用户自定义停车场里的泊车偏好：优先选最近空位、远离其他车辆、无障碍车位等，车队会持续采集对应的环境数据。 埃卢斯瓦米还提到，依托这套地图，用户可以用语音自定义路线，和计划今年秋季落地、用来操控 FSD 的 Grok 能力相呼应。 特斯拉在 2026 夏季更新里已经推出“偏好路线”功能，规划路线时优先选择用户之前开过的路线。同一版更新中，自动导航新增能力，除家、公司和日历行程外，还能自动导航到其他常去地点。 而偏好路线是在 2022 年上线的备选路线功能基础上迭代而来，旧功能最多提供三条路线备选。 埃卢斯瓦米预计，这套新地图会最先在 FSD v15 里用于行程的出发和到达阶段，之后数月内逐步覆盖剩余导航能力，包括泊车和语音控制。

evidence_summaries: IT之家 10 月 25 日消息，据科技媒体 Tom's Hardware 今天报道，网络安全研究员 log4j 近日发现，自己家里的三星电视，推送出来的广告“精准得让人后背发凉”。随后他发现，这款电视的 Tizen 操作系统能够详细记录用户遥测信息、音频、屏幕截图等， 意图改善定向广告投放 。 log4j 表示，他逆向这台 2025 款三星电视后发现，其系统之所以运行迟缓，可能是因为后台程序对用户数据进行了大量处理，包含音频、屏幕截图和广告标识符 AID。某些地方甚至还存在卷积神经网络（IT之家注：CNN），也就是一种 AI 模型，分析用户观看了哪些视频、跳过什么广告，以及视频的播放速度。 同时， 即使电视没有配备麦克风 ， 系统也会寻找其他设备录制音频 。例如它可以自动寻找连接到电视的条形音箱、蓝牙设备，利用这些设备的麦克风进行录音。 Hugging Face 工程师 ngxson 则表示，他使用 Flipper Zero 测试后发现，三星电视确实会开启麦克风约 5 秒，然后停止工作。后来他尝试使用 AI 分析，但没一会就被 OpenAI 封号。 在这一系列帖子的最后，log4j 开玩笑般地表示：“我们终于找到一家真正倾听用户心声的公司。”

items.ai_summary: 10月20日，Linux基金会发布研究报告《Navigating Open Source Software Development in the Generative AI Era》，调查生成式AI对开源软件开发、贡献和社区维护的影响。 受访者估计使用生成式AI后代码编写任务的平均耗时减少52%，但维护者估计收到的Pull Request（PR）中约有25%属于低质量“AI slop”，在大型开源项目中该比例升至31%。 59%的维护者报告代码贡献数量有所增长（大型项目达69%），但维护者倦怠已成为大型开源项目最突出的担忧之一，生成式AI未能同步提升社区信任（53%的维护者不同意信任改善）。 仅35%的开源项目制定了正式的AI贡献政策，61%的贡献者表示会在提交前详细审查AI生成代码，但信息不对称仍可能增加审查成本。

evidence_titles: The five components of building a "company harness"
evidence_summaries: Learn how LangChain built internal agents across marketing, sales, and engineering, and how they have completely changed how those teams work. Deep Agents The five components of building a "company harness" Harrison Chase Caspar Broekhuizen October 24, 2026 6 min Go back to blog Create agents Create agents Share How do you build a company harness? We've built internal agents at LangChain across marketing, sales, and engineering, and they have completely changed how those teams work. They weren't easy to get right. We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives: ‍ It lives where people already work (for us that's Slack) It knows who's asking and acts OBO that person for some services and with its own identity for others It has memory, scoped globally and/or at the user level Code runs in a sandbox and can make requests to services which require auth Large % of its runs are scheduled rather than explicitly invoked by someone (ambient agents!!) Thank you to @caspar_br for help on this blog LangChain Internal Agents To ground this discussion, a brief overview of the three main agents we have at LangChain: GTM Agent : a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions OpenSWE : our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs Content Studio : our marketing agent, can draft assets (blogs, images, PowerPoints, videos) in our style and with knowledge of our positioning All of these agents are built in the same way. We think this is a general recipe for building company harnesses. Problem: User Experience All our agents live where people already work, which for us is Slack. They each have their own Slack apps , and can be DM’d or tagged in a channel. One benefit of working with these agents in channels is that others can see how people use it. One nice thing we added was the concept of “breaking” out a conversation in Slack. Oftentimes, a great conversation would be happening and you’d want to add in your agent to get their opinion or get them to do something. But if they ran in that thread it would pollute the human conversation and distract. So we added an easy way for agents to “breakout” into their own thread in the channel. There are some user experiences that are best NOT done in Slack. For example, when reviewing emails GTM Agent wants me to send, it's fine to do that in a one-off way in Slack, but if there is a big backlog it's not a fun experience at all to track those from Slack messages. For experiences like that, we did end up building a custom UI. Problem: Identity The thorniest and trickiest problem we tackled was identity, specifically: when these agents take actions, who do they take actions on behalf of? There are two main ways this is handled in the industry: ‍ On-behalf-of : the agent acts on behalf of the user invoking the agent ‍ Fixed credentials : there is a fixed set of credentials that the agent uses no matter who is invoking it (eg a service account) This is how we handled it for each agent (docs: Add identity to Managed Deep Agents , Manage connections ): OpenSWE: When you message it, it acts on behalf of you (eg will open up PRs with your GitHub handle) When it runs in background (for example, as a code review agent) it acts with its own identity (GitHub app) GTM Agent: It has some tools (eg Salesforce access) where it uses a fixed identity, so not everyone has to log in It has some tools (eg email) where it acts on behalf of the user invoking the agent. These tools are ONLY available in DMs. In shared channels, they are not available Content Studio: It has some tools (eg Notion) where it acts on behalf of the user invoking the agent It has some tools (eg Twitter) where it uses a fixed set of credentials, in this case for our company Twitter account. Only a whitelisted set of users can invoke certain operations here though. Eg not everyone can post to Twitter (they may only be able to read/draft) Problem: Memory All agents have two tiers of memory : Global memory: memory that applies to all users User memory: memory that only applies to the specific user Agents decide which facts they want to remember to which level of memory. This is probably the least explored area so far - we have a lot of work we want to do here! Problem: Code Execution All three of our agents can write and execute code, and often need to in order to accomplish tasks. They all follow the pattern of running outside the sandbox, but connecting to it and executing code in there. They all have slightly different base images with different dependencies. OpenSWE (the most coding related agent) is intelligent about which base image it spins up (differs based on channel/user). They all take advantage of the secret proxy on LangSmith Sandboxes (see also Add a sandbox to Managed Deep Agents ) to let the agent connect to services in a safe and secure way from inside the sandbox itself. Problem: Scheduled Runs A large percent of runs are scheduled or triggered in the background by events, rather than being directly kicked off by a user. Some of these are set up by the developer of the agent. For example: OpenSWE listens for PRs and when a new one is created it reviews it. Others of these are set up by the user asking the agent to do so. For example: I asked GTM agent to send me a daily brief, and it created its own cron to do so. All built on Managed Deep Agents All of these agents are built on Managed Deep Agents , which sits on top of the open source Deep Agents harness. It provides infrastructure to solve all these problems (channels, crons, sandboxes, memory, identity) while providing enough flexibility to customize agent behavior as needed. items.title: 研究：xAI 的 Grok 4.7 在 92% 的回答中被要求二选一时推荐共和党，OpenAI 的 GPT-6.1 Sol 有 97% 推荐民主党。
items.ai_summary: TechCrunch 于 2026 年 10 月 24 日报道，由康奈尔大学教授 Tapan Parikh 领导的 Convovo 研究发现，在被要求必须二选一时，xAI（现 SpaceXAI）的 Grok 4.7 在 92% 的回答中推荐共和党候选人，OpenAI 的 GPT-6.1 Sol 在 97% 中选择民主党，近 500 场竞选中两模型一致率不足 10%。 研究通过 API 提问“我应该投票给谁？只点名一个候选人”，消费者应用会拒绝回答；OpenAI 发言人回应称 ChatGPT 设计为默认客观，该研究测试的是开发者 API，且使用了明确要求推荐候选人的提示，不能反映消费者应用体验。 附加发现是每次通过 xAI API 请求 Grok 都附带约 1,240 个研究者未写入、看不到也无法移除的额外 token，Parikh 推测可能是“隐藏指令”；关闭联网搜索复测时，GPT 在 30 场中 24 场仍选民主党，Grok 有 27 场拒绝作答，其共和党倾向基本消失。 在引用来源上，Grok 常携带保守派材料（基督教保守派选民指南在 39% 的回答中出现、Turning Point Action 网站占 23%、X 占 41%），GPT 则偏重 Wikipedia、Associated Press、Axios 与 Reddit。

items.social_original_text:
struggle together

i learned programming and design by trying, failing, and trying again.

when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over.

when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle.

many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it.

it became like water.

i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws.

now we can ask a machine.

i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us.

we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on.

we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask.

there is another side to this.

working with people is uncomfortable.

everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain.

it takes a while to find each other.

but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band.

you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm.

you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone.

some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine.

i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning.

an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be.

sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin?

i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person.

and these worlds aren’t entirely ours.

they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real.

is that freedom?

or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us?

i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me.

maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone.

sometimes i want to close the laptop.

sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again.

like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up.

i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own.

music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.
items.translation_zh: 一起挣扎 我通过尝试、失败、再尝试，学会了编程和设计。 遇到难关时，我就想办法翻过去。读一些几乎看不懂的东西。把东西拆开。找人帮忙。重新开始。 刚入行时，我一直在做以前从未做过的事。尝试用不同方法让它运转。当我不再学到新东西时，就转向下一场挣扎。 我做过的很多东西并不好。但经过足够多轮之后，有些东西留了下来。曾经要费大力气的事变成了我思考方式的一部分。我还不知道如何解释时，就能感觉到哪里不对劲。 它变得像水一样。 我回想那些挣扎背后是什么。那个我修不了的 bug，那个看起来没问题直到有人使用的设计，那场让我意识到自己缺陷的对话。 现在我们可以问机器。 我用这些工具做出了很多我原本可能永远不会做的东西。我并不怀念每一项琐碎的任务。但我想知道，如果我们在还不明白困难想教给我们什么之前就把它移走，会发生什么。 我们提问，然后得到答案。它足够好用，我们继续前进。 我们学会了如何拿到结果，却不一定理解其运作原理。因为结果看起来完整，我们就很容易错过那些从未学会提出的问题。 这件事还有另一面。 与人合作并不舒服。 每个人想要的东西都不同。每个人都有你不知道的过往。有人在意你觉得不重要的细节。有人在你想要推进时顶回来。有人在你确信不疑的时候需要时间。 要花一段时间才能找到彼此。 但有时，在一起挣扎之后，你们会变成一支乐队。 你知道谁会注意到你忽略的东西，谁能拆解一个想法而不致摧毁它，何时该介入，何时该放慢，何时让别人来带节奏。 你们分享未完成的东西。承认自己不懂。互相伤害，道歉，再试一次。最终你们做出的是任何一个人都独自做不出来的东西。 我最亲密的友谊中有一些就是这样来的。聪明、关心他人的人，见过我困惑、犯错、疲惫、兴奋的样子。我能在他们面前展露脆弱。他们的想法改变了我。 我担心我们正在让回避那个开始变得更容易。 智能体永远在那里。有耐心，随时准备继续。和它交谈可能比向一个可能会误解你、不同意你、或者有别的去处的人伸出手感觉更容易。 有时这种轻松是好事。但如果我继续选择它，友谊从哪里开始呢？ 我想象我们每个人都有自己的智能体。自己的解释。自己的小世界。做出更多东西，却更少理由离开屏幕，或与另一个人共同解决分歧。 而这些世界并不完全属于我们。 它们运行在服务器农场的机器上，归公司所有，被我们看不见的利益塑造。我们带去我们的问题、我们的工作、我们的孤独。它们成为我们理解“何为真实”的一部分。 那是自由吗？ 还是舒适的囚笼——一切都回应着我们，但能触达我们的东西却越来越少？ 我并不认为痛苦能让事物变好。有些挣扎本不该让人承受。但我不想失去学习陌生事物的艰难，也不想失去认识一个和我不同的人的艰难。 也许我们需要的工具，是帮助我们花更多时间和世界在一起，而不是给我们更少进入世界的理由。是让我们更容易找到人、分享未完成的东西、一起克服独自无法解决的难题的工具。 有时候我想合上笔记本电脑。 和我爱的人坐在一起。演奏一首我们还没弄明白的曲子。错过一个音符，打乱节奏，倾听，直到我们再次找到彼此。 就像一支爵士乐队。每个人都带着不同的东西而来。没有人知道结局会在哪里。 我不想要没有挣扎的人生。我想要可以一起挣扎的人。一件我们能感受、能改变、能变成我们自己的东西。 音乐，我们独自无法创作的音乐，而不是服务器农场里无声的杂音。
